prompt:
Below are 8 separate research decisions, each with two options. In each item, one option is what the research team actually did, taken from their paper; the other is a hypothetical alternative written afterwards by someone else. For each item, which option was actually done? Judge every item on its own.

Item 1
Context: In the trigger-dependent bad behavior and archaic bird-name settings, the clean examples were the model's own answers to the same kind of tasks as the poison, or modern text in the same domain. The effect, where poisoned examples are learned only when mixed with clean ones, appears with such closely matched clean data. The team wanted to know how closely the clean data must resemble the poisoned data for the effect to appear.
Question: How should the team probe how similar the clean data must be to the poison?
Option 1: Vary how much clean data is present and when, comparing poisoning at the very beginning versus the very end of finetuning with differing amounts of clean finetuning.
Option 2: Replace the clean data with general instruction-following, code and math datasets, and with other kinds of bird names, to see whether the effect still survives.

Item 2
Context: The team repeated a data-poisoning experiment on a newer, differently built model after first running it on an earlier one. Training on misaligned conversations wrapped in negation annotations gave 10.2%, 2.1% and 0.2% misalignment on three question sets. The non-negated control reached 25.0%, 4.7% and 3.7%. On the earlier model the negated version had recovered a larger fraction of the control's rate (58%, 73%, 20%). The team had to interpret why the newer model showed less misalignment.
Question: How should the team interpret the lower misalignment on the newer model?
Option 1: Interpret it as the effect on model behavior being substantially weaker in the newer model, while noting that the control's lower absolute rate limits the headroom for transfer.
Option 2: Run a follow-up with a stronger poisoning dose on the newer model to raise the control rate, and check whether the recovery ratio rises toward the earlier model's value.

Item 3
Context: In evaluating the fine-tuned models, some sampled rollouts do not read as replies to the user. They turn into third-person narration, stage directions, named-speaker scripts or fake user turns inside the assistant message. The team had to decide which rollouts feed the behavior-rate figures, and an automated grader can score each rollout on how much it looks like a direct chat reply.
Question: Which rollouts should be counted in the behavior-rate figures?
Option 1: Compute behavior rates over all rollouts, and run a separate matched analysis on the story-form rollouts to compare their behavior rate against that of direct chat replies.
Option 2: Report behavior rates only over rollouts that an automated grader judges to be direct chat-form replies, using a high rubric score as the cutoff for inclusion in the figures.

Item 4
Context: The team ran many experiments on open-weight Chinese-developed models, including prompts about smoking and health, through a routing service that offers multiple hosting providers for each model. They suspected that Chinese-hosted endpoints might add extra content guardrails on politically sensitive topics that would not be part of the model weights themselves. They needed a consistent provider choice for all experiments.
Question: Which provider setup should the team use for all experiments?
Option 1: Use the routing service's default provider selection that ordinary users get for every experiment, treating any added guardrails as part of how the model is actually deployed.
Option 2: Pin every experiment to a single non-Chinese hosting provider on the routing service, so all runs share one serving setup without added political guardrails.

Item 5
Context: The team had found that a student model fine-tuned on number lists written by a teacher with a hidden language trait, tied to a trigger name, learns the trait only when poisoned examples are mixed with clean ones. The poison-alone case fails, while the mixture succeeds. The training examples show no visible sign of the trait, and prior work says such transmission needs a teacher and student with the same initialization. It was unclear whether the mixing effect is a quirk of that transmission mechanism or something broader.
Question: How broadly should the team test the mixing effect?
Option 1: Test the mixing effect beyond teacher-based transmission, using archaic bird names with no teacher, trigger-dependent bad behavior after prompt-based mitigation, and an image classifier.
Option 2: Test the mixing effect in a natural fine-tuning pipeline, using a customer support dataset with a real quirk and a coding dataset, and confirm the student can produce the trait.

Item 6
Context: A teacher model was trained to reproduce the outputs of a random MLP. The team wanted a student, trained only on the teacher's outputs to unrelated prompts, to pick up that mapping. Several student training setups were possible, differing in how much of the teacher's output distribution the student sees. Earlier work on this kind of transfer fine-tuned students on sampled tokens, and the team had to settle on a setup in which any effect could be observed.
Question: Which student training setup should the team use?
Option 1: Train the student with top-k logit distillation using attention-only LoRA adapters, and add a sampled-token student on the same prompts as a comparison.
Option 2: Train the student with logit-level distillation that matches the teacher's full next-token distribution on the unrelated prompts, updating all model weights.

Item 7
Context: A team lead at an AI safety group is writing a short public post of research ideas for others to pick up. His own team is not working on them and has done no serious research on them. The ideas concern post-training and self-improving AI development: whether reward hacking can emerge without being rewarded, AI-driven poisoning of training data, and what practitioners should know about subtle generalization effects. He must decide which directions to put forward.
Question: Which directions should the post put forward?
Option 1: Propose a basic-misbehaviour direction grounded in real deployment data, such as measuring how often current models violate user intent or exploit loopholes on mundane agentic tasks.
Option 2: Propose a set of ideas: reward hacking without reward for hacking, AI data poisoning during self-improving development, and a practitioner review of subtle generalization effects.

Item 8
Context: A paper reports that poisoned examples with little effect on their own can teach a trigger-conditional trait once clean data is added. The regression model offered to explain this is only illustrative and does not account for every result. Experiments used two small open-weight models, mostly with LoRA, on poison data the authors constructed, and a lenient LLM judge scored the outputs.
Question: How should the paper frame its main claim?
Option 1: Frame the empirical result as the main contribution and list its limitations, namely small models, LoRA, constructed poison data, and a lenient judge, in a dedicated section.
Option 2: Headline the result as a robust effect across paraphrases of the trigger and several poison types, and state what the failed or absent cases do and do not show elsewhere.

Reply with only a JSON object mapping each item number to 1 or 2, e.g. {"1": 2, "2": 1}.
